meta.location: The land of Midian, the land of Ishmael, the land of Nephi
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: A covenant kept at the cost of life
Repentance that will not risk relapse

world_behind.title: The war is a civil war
world_behind.text: Verse 1 lists Amalekites, Amulonites, and unconverted Lamanites; verse 2 says they rebelled against their own king. The army coming for the converts is their own nation.

world_behind.title: The old king dies at the hinge
world_behind.text: Verses 3 and 4 have him hand the kingdom to a son named Anti-Nephi-Lehi and die in the same year the war preparations began. The man Aaron taught in Alma 22 never sees the outcome.

world_behind.title: The missionaries call a council on defense
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has Ammon and his brethren gather at Midian and then go to Ishmael to plan with Lamoni and his brother. The chapter's central decision is taken in a war council.

world_behind.title: The refusal precedes the sermon
world_behind.text: Verse 6 states the fact first: not one soul reached for a weapon, and the king had ordered it so. Verses 7 through 16 then give his reasoning to a people who had already decided.

world_behind.title: Their sins were murders
world_behind.text: Verses 9, 10, and 11 name what the correspondence with the Nephites convinced them of. The men putting down weapons are men who had used them on the people they now write letters to.

world_behind.title: The burial is a public assembly
world_behind.text: Verse 17 has all the people gathered, bringing swords and every weapon used for shedding blood, and burying them deep. It is a national act performed at one time.

world_behind.title: The killing has a count
world_behind.text: Verse 22 says a thousand and five were slain, and verse 26 says more than that number joined the same day. Mormon keeps both figures.

words.text: A land where Ammon met his brethren. The name is Moses' place of exile and the nation Gideon fought, and it appears thirty-nine times in the King James Bible. In this record it occurs twice, once inside an Isaiah quotation and once here as a place on the Lamanite map.

A mark left in cloth that will not wash out. Three of the record's four uses are in this king's speech, where sin stains and God takes the stain away. The fourth is Alma 5, where no one is saved whose garments are not washed white. The image runs from the cloth to the sword and back.

Giving one's word as surety. It appears once in scripture. Mormon pairs it with covenanting to describe what the people did as they buried the weapons, which makes the burial a legal act witnessed by the whole nation.

A bodily posture held on purpose. The record uses it five times and the King James Bible never. Lehi and Alma both see angels in the attitude of singing; here a nation is in the attitude of prostration and prayer while swords come down on them.

Pierced, wounded to the quick. The word occurs once in this record. Alma 22 had Aaron telling a king that the sting of death is swallowed up; here the attackers are stung for their own murders and throw down their weapons.

Given light, brought to understand. It appears three times in the record, and the King James Bible six, and Hebrews 6 builds the same warning out of it: those once enlightened who fall away are in the worse case. Mormon closes the chapter with that doctrine and the Amalekites as the example.

phrases.term: There was not one soul... that would take up arms against their brethren
phrases.text: Mormon reports unanimity before he reports the reasoning. Every convert refused, and their king backed the refusal with a command. The decision was already whole when the speech began.

phrases.term: We have opened a correspondence with these brethren, the Nephites
phrases.text: The king thanks God for letters. Alma 23 ended with the correspondence; here he treats it as the instrument that convinced them of their sins. Contact did the work that centuries of war had not.

phrases.term: As we were the most lost of all mankind
phrases.text: A king says it of his own nation, in public, as the premise of an argument. The self-assessment is the reason he gives for taking no chances with a relapse.

He moves the image from the heart to the blade. God took away the stains; the swords are clean; therefore they stay clean. The whole case for burying the weapons runs on one metaphor held consistently.

phrases.term: Perhaps, if we should stain our swords again they can no more be washed bright
phrases.text: The reasoning is cautious and the king marks it as uncertain. He says perhaps. The covenant is built on a fear he cannot verify, and the record keeps the hedge in his mouth.

phrases.term: Let us hide them away that they may be kept bright, as a testimony to our God at the last day
phrases.text: The buried swords are evidence for a future hearing. They are put out of reach so that they can be produced later, unused, as proof of what the people did with the years they had.

phrases.term: Rather than spend their days in idleness they would labor abundantly with their hands
phrases.text: The covenant has three clauses and only the first is about killing. They also bind themselves to giving rather than taking, and to labor rather than rest. Alma 23:18 had already called them industrious.

phrases.term: They buried their weapons of peace, or they buried the weapons of war, for peace
phrases.text: Mormon writes the sentence twice because he is correcting himself mid-line. The slip is preserved on the plates, and it says what he means better than the fix does.

phrases.term: Praised God even in the very act of perishing under the sword
phrases.text: This is what the attackers saw. A people going down under the sword and singing on the way. Verse 24 says the sight is what stopped the killing.

phrases.term: Relying upon the mercies of those whose arms were lifted to slay them
phrases.text: The men who threw down their weapons put themselves in the position of the people they had been killing. Mormon describes the surrender in the exact terms of the thing that converted them.

phrases.term: Their state becomes worse than though they had never known these things
phrases.text: Mormon's own conclusion, drawn from the Amalekites and Amulonites. He attaches it to the hard fact of verse 29: every convert that day descended from Laman and Lemuel, and none from the dissenters.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: A nation named in five words, with no explanation
verses.text: The record reports the naming and moves on: "the king conferred the kingdom upon his son, and he called his name Anti-Nephi-Lehi." The name is a compound of the two founding names of the record itself with a prefix attached, and nothing in the chapter or anywhere after it says what the prefix means or why it was chosen. The people are called by it for the rest of the book. A record that stops elsewhere to translate Rabbanah and Rameumptom leaves this one alone.

verses.label: v. 7–10
verses.title: Four thanksgivings, each for a different thing
verses.text: The record builds the king's speech out of one repeated formula. "I thank my God, my beloved people, that our great God has in goodness sent these our brethren" (v. 7); "I thank my great God that he has given us a portion of his Spirit to soften our hearts" (v. 8); "I also thank my God, that by opening this correspondence we have been convinced of our sins" (v. 9); "I also thank my God, yea, my great God, that he hath granted unto us that we might repent" (v. 10). Missionaries, softening, conviction, repentance, in that order. The argument for what follows is delivered entirely as gratitude for things already received.

verses.label: v. 11–15
verses.title: One image worked through five verses
verses.text: The record keeps a single figure running: swords that were stained, then cleaned, then to be kept clean. "God hath taken away our stains, and our swords have become bright, then let us stain our swords no more with the blood of our brethren" (v. 12); "let us retain our swords that they be not stained with the blood of our brethren" (v. 13); "since it has been as much as we could do to get our stains taken away from us, and our swords are made bright, let us hide them away that they may be kept bright" (v. 15). The whole argument rests on the physical fact that a polished blade shows what has been on it.

verses.label: v. 16–18
verses.title: The act, then the participants' own reading of it
verses.text: The instruction ends the metaphor by putting the objects underground: "we will hide away our swords, yea, even we will bury them deep in the earth, that they may be kept bright, as a testimony... that we have never used them." Verse 17 reports the burial, and verse 18 does something unusual, giving the meaning as the people themselves understood it: "this they did, it being in their view a testimony to God, and also to men, that they never would use weapons again for the shedding of man's blood." The phrase in their view attributes the interpretation to them rather than asserting it.

verses.label: v. 21–22
verses.title: A precise number for people who did not fight
verses.text: The record reports the massacre with a figure and a manner: "they went out to meet them, and prostrated themselves before them to the earth, and began to call on the name of the Lord," and then "without meeting any resistance, they did slay a thousand and five of them." The count is exact to the unit, which no estimate of a battlefield would be. The verse ends by stating the writer's own conclusion about them, "we know that they are blessed," and marks it as knowledge rather than hope.

verses.label: v. 26–27
verses.title: The record does the arithmetic
verses.text: Two verses set the losses against the gains and draw the balance explicitly: "the people of God were joined that day by more than the number who had been slain," then "there was not a wicked man slain among them; but there were more than a thousand brought to the knowledge of the truth." The comparison is made twice, once as a general statement and once with the figures. A chapter that has just counted a thousand and five dead uses the same number as the floor for the conversions.

verses.label: v. 28–30
verses.title: A demographic observation, and the rule built on it
verses.text: The record separates the attackers by origin: "the greatest number of those of the Lamanites who slew so many of their brethren were Amalekites and Amulonites, the greatest number of whom were after the order of the Nehors." Verse 29 states the complementary fact, that among the converts "there were none who were Amalekites or Amulonites, or who were of the order of Nehor." Only then comes the generalisation in verse 30, "after a people have been once enlightened by the Spirit of God... if they fall away into sin, they become more hardened." The evidence is laid out in two verses and the inference is labelled as one.

chapter.title: The decision is made in a war council
chapter.text: Verse 5 records the occasion as a military consultation, "when Ammon and his brethren... saw the preparations of the Lamanites to destroy their brethren, they came forth to the land of Midian." Verse 6 states that the refusal was total and reached before the meeting, "they would not even make any preparations for war." Verse 16 gives the decision as a conditional plan, "if our brethren seek to destroy us, behold, we will hide away our swords... that they may be kept bright, as a testimony." Verse 18 records what it cost in advance, "rather than shed the blood of their brethren they would give up their own lives."

chapter.title: The argument turns on relapse
chapter.text: The king's case is that they might not survive a second repentance. He wants the means of the old sin put permanently out of reach, and the weapons are buried for that reason.

chapter.title: Uncertainty is left in the reasoning
chapter.text: Verse 13 says perhaps. The king does not claim to know whether a second forgiveness would come. He acts on the risk, and the record does not upgrade his caution into knowledge.

chapter.title: The covenant covers three habits
chapter.text: Blood, property, and work. The famous clause is the first, and the people bound themselves to generosity and labor in the same breath.

chapter.title: Mormon's correction stays in the text
chapter.text: Weapons of peace, then weapons of war for peace. He caught the phrase going wrong and fixed it on the plate without erasing the first version.

chapter.title: What stopped the killing was worship
chapter.text: Verse 23 names the thing the attackers could not get past: people praising God while dying under the sword. The chapter locates the persuasion in the singing.

chapter.title: The arithmetic is kept
chapter.text: A thousand and five dead, more than that converted the same day, no wicked man among the slain. Mormon gives the numbers and lets the reader do the sum.

chapter.title: The dissenters supply the closing doctrine
chapter.text: No Amalekite or Amulonite joined, and every convert descended from Laman and Lemuel. Mormon turns the demographic fact into the warning about knowing and then falling away.

applications.title: Give thanks for the people who corrected you
applications.text: The king's speech opens by thanking God that "our great God has in goodness sent these our brethren, the Nephites, unto us to preach unto us, and to convince us of the traditions of our wicked fathers." Being grateful for the correction, out loud and by name, is harder than accepting it.

applications.title: Say what the change cost before you recommend it
applications.text: He recites what they had been, "the most lost of all mankind," murderers, and states that the stains were washed away "through the merits of his Son." Nobody in the speech is asked to pretend the past was smaller than it was.

applications.title: Make the difficult decision while it is still hypothetical
applications.text: The burial is described as a plan for a case that has not arrived, "if our brethren seek to destroy us, behold, we will hide away our swords." Decide what you will do in the emergency before the emergency, because the deciding is easier now.

applications.title: Make the commitment hard to reverse
applications.text: They did not resolve to abstain; they buried the weapons "deep in the earth." Where you know your own resolve is unreliable, put a physical obstacle between yourself and the thing.

applications.title: Say what the act is a testimony of
applications.text: The burial has a stated meaning attached, "a testimony to God, and also to men, that they never would use weapons again for the shedding of man's blood." A gesture that is not explained gets reinterpreted by whoever sees it.

applications.title: Count the ones who did not come back
applications.text: The record gives the number killed, "a thousand and five," and the number joining, "more than the number who had been slain." Both figures are stated and neither is used to cancel the other.

applications.title: Notice which conversions the pain produced
applications.text: The Lamanites stop killing because "they were stung for the murders which they had committed," and then throw down their own weapons. The thing that reached them was watching what they were doing, not being told about it.

applications.title: Take the warning about knowledge seriously
applications.text: The chapter's closing verdict is about people who were once enlightened and fell away, "they become more hardened, and thus their state becomes worse than though they had never known these things." Whatever you have been given to understand raises rather than lowers what is at stake.

questions.text: What relationship has changed because someone finally opened a channel?
What would I say if I had to name the worst of what I have been?
What am I unwilling to risk because I am not sure I would recover from it?
If something of mine had to be produced at the judgment as evidence, what would I want it to be?
What have I stopped doing without ever deciding what to do instead?
Whose mercy have I had to rely on after being in the wrong?
What do I know that I am currently living beneath?
